clue.text: Unable to escape, in huff, danced atrociously

indicators.note: Doing a thing atrociously is doing it badly, and letters handled badly will not stay in the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters — exactly the length the grid wants

explanation.surface: Somebody flouncing off in a temper and then dancing very badly indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: Counting settles it: 'huff danced' is exactly ten letters, so 'in' can only be joinery and the definition has to stop at 'escape'.
explanation.definitionFit: Handcuffed describes a person whose wrists are locked together, which is precisely being unable to escape: adjective for adjective phrase.

clue.text: Journalist cut

definitions.meaning: the newspaper sense: a writer turning out routine copy to order
the axe sense: to chop at a thing with rough, uneven strokes

explanation.surface: A reporter caught by the newsroom's staff cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is nearly always two definitions, since there is no room for anything else; the work is noticing that the two words come from different worlds, Fleet Street and the woodpile.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is a jobbing reporter, said with a sneer; and to hack is to cut at something with rough chopping blows.

clue.text: Wine stains covering cosy spot

indicators.note: Stains that cover something spread across it and hide what lies beneath, which is what these two words are doing to four consecutive letters.

parts.note: four letters running on from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Red wine spreading across the upholstery of a comfortable corner.
explanation.walkthrough: The hiding place is the first two words, which read as one ordinary noun phrase and so get skimmed. 'Covering' is the only word asking you to look at letters rather than at furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest is the snug hollow a bird builds and settles down into, so 'cosy spot' is the word's plainest sense.

clue.text: Harms, actual but not bodily?

definitions.meaning: reads as legal boilerplate: actual bodily harm, ABH, is a charge in English criminal law, and the clue has taken the phrase apart
the setter's reading: this harm is done at a distance, to systems and records rather than to a person

explanation.surface: A lawyer working out exactly what kind of harm has been done, and to whom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Actual bodily harm' is a specific offence in English law, and the clue dismantles it: keep the harm and the actual, drop the bodily, and what is left is damage done down a wire.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyberattacks do real damage — to money, data, reputations — without anybody being touched, so they are harms that are actual but not bodily.

clue.text: Apartment: better capital investment

parts.note: a flat is the British word for an apartment
to cap a performance is to better it, to go one higher

explanation.surface: An estate agent pitching a smart apartment as a shrewd place to put your money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital investment' is doing no financial work at all — both words are being used in senses the money page never uses, and the colon after 'Apartment' is the only punctuation the wordplay needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Capital is Latin for 'of the head' and to invest is to clothe, so the phrase means head-covering — which a flat cap is.

clue.text: One absconding from starters of steak and kidney pies, you say?

indicators.note: you say tells us the letter names are spoken and the word they sound like is the answer

parts.words: starters of steak and kidney pies
parts.note: the opening letters of steak, kidney and pies are S, K, P, said aloud as the letter names ess-kay-pee

explanation.surface: Someone running off from a plate of steak and kidney pie starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Spell out the initials S, K, P and say them aloud: ess-kay-pee. 'and' is only a link here, so its A is not used. Steak and kidney pie is a classic British pub dish.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapee is a person who has broken free, so it is someone who has absconded or fled.

clue.text: Junk messages: plans to return?

definitions.note: Spam is a mass noun: the single word covers any number of the messages at once, so a plural definition lands on an answer that looks singular.

indicators.note: To return is to come back the way you went, so the four letters just named are read back from their far end.

parts.note: plans of a route or a town are maps

explanation.surface: An email asking whether the plans everyone was promised are coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon is doing the joining, so 'junk messages: plans' never was one phrase about an inbox however hard the surface pushes it that way.
explanation.definitionFit: Spam is the collective name for unsolicited bulk email, which is what junk messages are in their everyday computing sense.

clue.text: Concerning hobby having enormous familiarity with The Queen's Head

definitions.meaning: reads as a pastime that has taken somebody over completely — the wrong sort of familiarity altogether
the setter's reading: on the surface that is a pub name, but on a British stamp it is the sovereign's profile, printed on every single one

explanation.surface: A man so devoted to his hobby, and to the pub called The Queen's Head, that everybody there knows him.
explanation.walkthrough: British definitive stamps carry nothing but the monarch's head in profile, so a collector meets that one image thousands of times over. The pub sign is the decoy, and the capital letters are what sell it.
explanation.definitionFit: Philatelic means to do with stamp collecting, and British stamps carry the monarch's head, so the hobby is one long acquaintance with that profile.

clue.text: This person's business? On the contrary, don't mention it

indicators.note: 'On the contrary' asks for the opposite of the word just given, and there is one standing opposite in the phrase that always pairs them.

parts.note: the setter pointing at himself, so 'this person's' is a first-person possessive
'business or pleasure' is the standing pair, so the contrary of the first word is the second

explanation.surface: Somebody brushing off a nosy question about their line of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This person's' is the crossword's way of writing 'my' without writing I, and the two halves only join because 'business or pleasure' is a phrase everybody finishes automatically.
explanation.definitionFit: 'My pleasure' is the set reply to thanks, swappable word for word with 'don't mention it' — a whole-phrase idiom rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Pierce, cut into melon somewhere on Atlantic coast

indicators.note: the shortened verb goes into the melon

parts.note: a casaba is a variety of winter melon

indicators.note: cut means trimmed, so the last letter of the verb is lopped off

parts.note: to lance is to pierce, as a boil

explanation.surface: Someone named Pierce slices into a melon, as if in a kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pierce' looks like a name but is the verb LANCE; 'cut' trims it to LANC, which goes into CASABA.
explanation.definitionFit: Casablanca is the large Moroccan port city facing the Atlantic Ocean.

clue.text: In this manner of speaking, power comes forth

definitions.meaning: reads as 'so to speak', the phrase people put in front of a figure of speech; here it means literally a way of talking
the setter's reading: say FORCE, meaning power, with the s gone soft, and out comes 'forth'

explanation.surface: A grand pronouncement that strength is on its way at last.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not describe the answer so much as perform it: 'power' is FORCE, and FORCE said with a soft s is the very word the clue prints.
explanation.definitionFit: A lisp is the speech habit that softens an s towards a th, so it is exactly the manner of speaking the clue is demonstrating on itself.

clue.text: Bullion and cash man's collected — here?

definitions.text: Bullion and cash man's collected — here?

parts.note: bullion is gold in bars

indicators.note: collected here means gathered up and put together afresh, so the letters of the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A banker's stash of gold bars and cash being gathered at some financial institution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected' reads as gathered up, as bullion is in a vault, but here it rearranges the letters of cash and man's. The whole clue also describes the bank, a place full of gold and money.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldman Sachs is a major American investment bank, the sort of place where gold and money are amassed.

clue.text: Cook's directions describing flipping Mexican food, right to do the same?

indicators.note: A circle described around a thing encloses it, so the outer word is drawn right around what comes next.

parts.note: a recipe is a cook's set of directions, and it is the word that gets opened up

indicators.note: Flipping turns a thing over so it faces the other way, and letters flipped are read from their far end back.

parts.note: the Mexican food in question, before it is turned over
r is the standard abbreviation for right, and it joins the food before the pair are flipped together

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions about turning a taco the right way and then doing it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right to do the same' reads as one phrase of approval, and that is where the definition hides: only the last four words define, while 'right' belongs to the wordplay as a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To reciprocate is to return a favour in kind — to do the same back — and both are infinitive verb phrases you could swap over.

clue.text: Authority's laughable admonition

indicators.note: Something laughable has been made ridiculous, and a word made ridiculous has had its letters knocked out of their proper places.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters — the very ten the grid asks for

explanation.surface: A ticking-off so feeble that everyone finds it funny.
explanation.walkthrough: A single long word supplying every letter is the hardest anagram to spot: there is nothing to add and nothing to drop, so the eye reads the word instead of counting it.
explanation.definitionFit: Domination is control exercised over other people, which is authority in its heavier sense — power held rather than power granted.

clue.text: N African to pick up engaging eagle that's flapping

indicators.note: engaging here means holding or enclosing, so the first word takes the second inside it

parts.note: to sense something is to pick it up, as with a signal or a mood

indicators.note: a bird that's flapping is moving wildly, so its letters are tossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A North African who is trying to catch an eagle beating its wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's flapping' rearranges eagle, and 'engaging' puts the result inside the word for pick up. 'engaging' looks like an adjective meaning charming, but it signals containment.
explanation.definitionFit: A Senegalese person comes from Senegal, a country on the north-west African coast.

clue.text: Clear absolutely minimal amount of money — and leave too much

parts.note: overt means out in the open, clear for anybody to see
the smallest British coin is one penny, written 1p on a price tag, and the numeral is typed here as a letter I

explanation.surface: Somebody perfectly open about having barely a coin, who then leaves far too much behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Absolutely minimal amount of money' is a description of a coin rather than an instruction, and the coin arrives spelled the way a price tag spells it, with a numeral standing in for a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To overtip is to leave a larger gratuity than the bill deserves, so 'leave too much' is the same verb with the tip understood.

clue.text: Some recommend Les Six as eternal

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, which is how a run of letters inside the words gets flagged.

parts.note: seven letters running on from inside the first word, through the whole of the second, into the start of the third

explanation.surface: A few critics putting the French composers Les Six forward as music for all time.
explanation.walkthrough: Les Six were a group of six French composers gathered round Poulenc and Milhaud, and the capitals and italics are there to send you thinking about music instead of counting letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Endless means having no end, which is what eternal means of time — the same adjective, one plain and one Latinate.

clue.text: Independent republic, 'Éire' label acknowledging nature's divinity, originally?

definitions.text: Independent republic, 'Éire' label acknowledging nature's divinity, originally?

indicators.note: What a word is originally is the letter it starts from, so every word in the list gives up its opening and nothing else.

parts.note: the first letter of Independent
the first letter of republic
the first letter of Éire, the state's name in Irish
the first letter of label
the first letter of acknowledging
the first letter of nature's
the first letter of divinity

explanation.surface: A republic's paperwork: the name it uses in its own language, and a nod to the sacredness of the natural world.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word does two jobs at once — the sentence describes the country and its initials spell it — and Éire is simply what the state calls itself in Irish, so the accent is not decoration.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: Ireland is an independent republic, labelled Éire in its own language, with an old reverence for the divinity of the natural world.

clue.text: Deserts' shortcomings

definitions.meaning: the verb, third person: a soldier or a spy abandons his own side and goes over to the enemy
the noun, plural: the faults and failings that stop a thing being up to standard

explanation.surface: The drawbacks of life in the Sahara.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the whole misdirection: it turns 'deserts' into a possessive full of sand when the word is really a verb, and the two definitions simply stand side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: One defects when one deserts one's own side for the other; and defects are shortcomings, the faults in a thing — a verb and a plural noun sharing a spelling.

clue.text: Furious Grizelda sacking Dutch tradesperson

indicators.note: furious means wild with rage, so the remaining letters are thrown about
sacking someone means getting rid of them, so the letter for Dutch is removed from the name

explanation.surface: An angry employer named Grizelda firing her Dutch worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sacking Dutch' removes D from GRIZELDA to give GRIZELA, which 'Furious' rearranges. 'Dutch' reads as an adjective describing the tradesperson, but it is only the letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: A glazier fits glass in windows and doors, a skilled trade, so the word names a tradesperson.

clue.text: Dour expert's frown

parts.note: grim means dour, forbidding, without a scrap of cheer
an ace at something is an expert at it

explanation.surface: A humourless specialist pulling a face at what he has been shown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dour expert' reads as one person, and the apostrophe-s that follows is not a possessive at all but the verb 'is' — the small join that turns two words into a sum.
explanation.definitionFit: A grimace is a face twisted in distaste or pain, which is what a frown is — the same noun for the same expression.

clue.text: Baked goods all gone, according to Spooner: porkies!

indicators.note: Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words, so the first sounds of lack and pies trade places

parts.note: when something is all gone there is a lack of it; said aloud, a lack of runs together as a-lack-ov
pies are baked goods

explanation.surface: A bakery has sold out of everything, followed by an outraged cry of disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'a lack of pies' and swap the L and P sounds. 'Porkies' is British rhyming slang: porky pies rhymes with lies.
explanation.definitionFit: Porkies are falsehoods in British slang, so a whole bunch of untruths is a set of porkies.

clue.text: For the most part, walk dragging leg: b___ leg!

indicators.note: for the most part means most but not all, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to limp is to walk unevenly, dragging an injured leg
the letter b shown with the rest of the word blanked out, giving just B

explanation.surface: Hobbling along with a bad leg, someone swears at the leg in question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the most part' cuts LIMP to LIM; the 'b___' gives just its B. The blanked word looks like a censored curse at the bad leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A limb is an arm or a leg, so a leg is one example of a limb.

clue.text: Revolting sung play's regularly rejected

indicators.note: Letters rejected at regular intervals means every other one is thrown away, and whatever survives is read in the order it stands.

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of those two words run together; the odd-numbered ones are the ones discarded

explanation.surface: An opera nobody will stage, turned down again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected' looks like an instruction to reverse and is nothing of the kind: it says which letters to throw away, and the survivors read left to right just as they stand.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugly means repellent to look at, and revolting is that same reaction a degree stronger — both adjectives for a thing you turn away from.

clue.text: Everyman endlessly late: fancy!

parts.note: Everyman is the setter, and a setter refers to themself as I

indicators.note: endlessly means without an end, so the final letter is cut off

parts.note: the late means dead, as in the late king

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the setter being forever late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' as in 'the late Mr Smith' means DEAD, which 'endlessly' trims to DEA. 'fancy' reads as an exclamation of surprise but is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy is a notion or whim that comes into the mind, so it is an idea.

clue.text: Scoring — or practising turntablism?

definitions.meaning: the plain sense: dragging something sharp across a surface and leaving marks behind
the hip-hop sense: a DJ working a vinyl record back and forth beneath the stylus to make a rhythm out of it

explanation.surface: A note on what the man behind the record decks is actually doing.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are gerunds, which is what lets them sit either side of the dash as though they were alternatives — and a needle dragged through a groove really is scoring the vinyl.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring means marking a surface with a sharp point; scratching is also the DJ's trick of rocking a record under the needle, which is turntablism.

clue.text: On the one hand, finally, Miss …

indicators.note: 'Finally' asks for the letter each word finishes on, taken in the order the words arrive.

parts.note: the last letter of On
the last letter of the
the last letter of one
the last letter of hand

explanation.surface: One side of an argument being weighed up, and a young lady addressed at the end of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the one hand' is such a fixed phrase that it gets read as a unit instead of as four separate words, and the capital M on 'Miss' is the sentence's doing, not a title's.
explanation.definitionFit: To need someone is to feel their absence, which is what missing them amounts to — the same verb in the same plain form.

clue.text: Rowdy boys 'silent', so it would appear

indicators.note: A rowdy crowd will not stand in line, and neither will the letters this word has been put in front of.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A gang of loud boys putting on a display of being perfectly quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks round 'silent' are the setter's nudge that the word is material rather than description, while 'rowdy boys' is the picture doing all the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Ostensibly means as far as appearances go, with the hint that the truth is otherwise — which is exactly what 'so it would appear' concedes.
